reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that strong default hyperparameters—learned through meta-training on 118 tabular datasets—can rival or exceed per-dataset HPO in both accuracy and efficiency. This is formalized as a decision-theoretic optimization over time-accuracy tradeoffs. Let θ_td denote the vector of meta-tuned defaults, and let D_meta_train be the training set of 118 datasets. Then, for any new dataset D_new, we define a loss function L(D_new, θ_td) = E[loss(f(x; θ_td), y)] where f is the predictive model. The key innovation is that these defaults are chosen such that they minimize expected loss on D_meta_test, a disjoint and more extreme benchmark. Algorithm selection over defaults is modeled as a multi-armed bandit or greedy policy over empirical risk estimates r_a = L(D_meta_test, θ_a). If the time-cost t_a is also bounded, then the optimal policy maximizes utility U = α·r_a − β·t_a for suitable weights α, β. The failure mode arises when D_new lies outside the support of D_meta_train, leading to poor generalization. To mitigate this, era-conditioned defaults introduce a regime classifier c_e that partitions the hyperparameter space into θ_e, allowing adaptation to non-stationary environments. This is a form of inductive bias that improves robustness under distribution shift.
